utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's wait for Mr. Brdjanin, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, good afternoon you. Appearances, Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: David Cunningham, John Ackerman, and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. I understand there are some preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, there are, Your Honour. The first one goes back to the discussion we had with Your Honours last week about the question of an appeal. As Your Honours know we filed an appeal last Wednesday, within the seven days, and now the situation arises that although we've asked for an expedited hearing because of the importance, what the situation will be as regards joint enterprise in its third category for the remainder of the trial until such time as the appeal is heard. Because as Your Honour said two weeks ago, for all purposes we're precluded now from addressing any further submissions to Your Honours on it. Mr. Ackerman at this stage is entitled to proceed, unless Your Honours say otherwise, because of the appeal is entitled to proceed on the basis he doesn't have to concern himself with that aspect. So I raise it now so Your Honours can make a decision perhaps -- preferably before we adjourn, but if not at the beginning of the next session, in the new year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. I think it can be addressed. Let me hear what Mr. Ackerman has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't anticipate that this would come up, so I really have nothing to say. As far as I'm concerned, a decision by a Trial Chamber is a binding decision. I think it's not in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole thing boils down to what our law is or how our law stands on matters of execution of judgements pending appeal. That's what it boils down to. And I think it is sufficiently addressed in the Rules already. Give it a thought, Mr. Ackerman, as well, and at your earliest please come back to us if you have any comments. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's why I raised it. Your Honour, the second matter is this: Yesterday when we were dealing with the timetable, Your Honours said that we should file our final briefs by the 31st of March, Mr. Ackerman the 1st of April. Mr. Ackerman mentioned that that didn't give time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- to respond to us, but Your Honours in fact the practice is this. We both file on the same day, and then if either wishes to respond to matters that are in the other side's brief, we apply to Your Honour for leave. So I would ask that we both file on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Your Honour, as long as there's an opportunity to respond to their brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. As I tried to explain yesterday, you will find us very flexible on that. So for us it doesn't really make a difference. I suppose Mr. Roberts is following the proceedings, as he did yesterday, and he will jot this down and we'll discuss it when we have the Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But take it for granted that is all find us very flexible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful. It seemed to be most sensible. That will give both sides to deal with matters that are raised. And finally, Your Honours, this: I sent Mr. Ackerman an email yesterday setting out a sort of proposed list of sites and places for any visits that Your Honour may make, and I hope Mr. Ackerman got it. Well, in that case, I'm not sure about his email address. All right. I think I also copied it to Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Still trying to figure out how to get to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls has one matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to raise this in private session, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: With respect to the next witness, the next witness I believe is arriving today. We're going to proof that witness tomorrow morning, and we will be ready to put him on as soon as this witness is over. So I hope it won't break anyone's heart to move that witness up maybe to Wednesday rather than Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, the earlier we're finished the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it's unlikely that I'm going to finish with whatever I have left today, after the direct finishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see where we get and take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just before the witness -- when is Your Honour intending to have this Status Conference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was thinking of Thursday, but -- I was thinking initially of Wednesday, but I thought you had some problems on Wednesday. And I'll try and accommodate you as much as I can. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, such problems as we have are not ones which ought to take precedence over what Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's easier for everyone to have the Status Conference on Thursday, we'll try and have it on Thursday. Yes, please, could you bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. We are continuing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- with your testimony today. And I'm just reminding you that you are testifying under the solemn undertaking that you made yesterday; namely, to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off yesterday we were talking about the ARK Crisis Staff, and we were talking about the 15 members from Banja Luka. What I'd like to do now is talk to you about the physical plant, the facilities of the ARK Crisis Staff. Where did the ARK Crisis Staff meet at?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis staff of the ARK met in an office in the municipal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. assembly building in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Who did that office belong to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It belonged to the municipal authorities of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the ARK Crisis Staff ever had its own office?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You, in your capacity as the vice-president of the ARK Crisis Staff, did you have anyone who worked for you? Anyone that was your assistant?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you aware of anyone who worked for the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us when you found out you were appointed to the ARK Crisis Staff you found out by way of a telephone call. How were you notified of ARK Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually by phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what would those telephone calls inform you of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have a meeting of the crisis staff at the following time in the following room.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Would the phone call include anything about the agenda or the matters to be discussed at the next meeting of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Before you attended a meeting of the ARK Crisis Staff, were you ever given any documents, an agenda? Was that supplied to you before you attended?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Upon your arrival at the meetings, would any documents be passed out to the members of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time, not .

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. How would it be, then, that you and other members of the crisis staff would be notified as to what would be the subjects of discussion for that meeting? How did you find out about an agenda, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a meeting starts, someone puts forward the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And who would be the individual putting forth the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: At the meetings, five or six meetings you attended, who was the presiding individual at the ARK Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you said once a meeting starts, someone puts forward the agenda. Please describe, if you can, how Mr. Brdjanin would put forward the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would open the meeting. He had documents in front of him. I don't know whether it was typed up or not. And then he would set the agenda for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Would he set the agenda -- let me back up. Could other individuals, other members -- other individuals who were attending the crisis staff, could they suggest items for the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And can you give us an example of a situation where a topic was suggested and added to the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall any specific ones right now, off the bat. But I think there were such cases, just that I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you know an individual by the name of Boro Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at the time he was the secretary to the Assembly of the ARK. He was a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did he have any connection to the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him at meetings. Therefore, I don't know if he had any connection or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone was tasked or given the responsibility of taking the minutes of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone inside the meetings taking notes, taking what appeared to be minutes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice anyone taking the minutes in any common, widespread sense of the word, but there probably was someone doing that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you during this short period of time that this entity existed, did you ever see any minutes from the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the early part of the existence of the ARK Crisis Staff, how were the meetings conducted? You've told us that Mr. Brdjanin would preside over the meetings. But what would happen once the agenda was set?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting would start.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And once it would start, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually the president of the crisis staff talked about problems, assessments. There would be conclusions proposed at the end -- towards the end of each session, and other members of the crisis staff took part in the work of the session, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How would a conclusion be adopted, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a way, a peculiar way. He asked us whether we were in favour or not. There was no particular procedure adopted for this, in the usual sense of the word. He would just consult us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we talked about the one exhibit that listed 15 members of the crisis staff, all from Banja Luka. Was there a time when the composition of the crisis staff changed from those 15 members?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at it yesterday, and I'm familiar with the composition. I believe that Mr. Kuzmanovic was replaced, but I don't know whether he attended any of the meetings. At least, I never saw him there. Secondly, I know that many members didn't even come when I was there, so sometimes there would be someone else coming on behalf of someone else; someone on behalf of Zupljanin, for example. But not everyone attended, and a good many of those who held official positions were sometimes not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you know why it is that those who held official positions were not coming to crisis staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I know that when I couldn't make it, I just wasn't there, for official reasons or other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If we look at Exhibit 168, which is the list of the members of the crisis staff, if we look at entry number 16, it says: "Presidents of the municipalities." Do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixteen; Presidents. The Rip Municipality; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Now, at any time while the crisis staff was in existence, did you notice that its composition had changed to representatives of the various municipalities within the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when was that? Was that towards the beginning, the middle, or towards the end of the existence of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, that was June, towards the end of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Can you describe these meetings, what were the topics of conversation? First of all, let's talk about how the agenda was set. Was it set the same way you described, by Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in almost the same way, with the proviso that at those meetings you had representatives from the municipalities, not from all the municipalities. And sometimes you had two or three people coming from the same municipality. So it was a sort of a meeting the way I viewed it, and I did not consider it to be a meeting of the crisis staff. It was just a meeting, a gathering of people, people who came to discuss problems in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You talked about how there would be people from some but not all of the municipalities within the ARK. What sort of topics would they raise during these discussions, these meetings that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would bring up a wide range of different subjects; the economy, the problems they were facing in their everyday lives, the Krajina area being surrounded, for example. There was still no way out of the area towards the mother country at that point. They talked about problems to do with refugees, with collection centres, with general safety, with the supplies running out, with medical supplies running out, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You talked about -- let's talk about the supplies that you just referenced, the supplies running out and the medical supplies coming out. When these representatives would come to these meetings, would they make any requests with respect to supplies?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were requests being made by those representatives who were in need of certain kinds of supplies. I believe the council of the ARK helped with that, with the commodity reserves, with fuel supplies, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you say "the council of the ARK," are you talking about the executive council?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And who was the head of the executive council?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nikola Erceg.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You also talked about how the municipality members would talk about general safety. During these meetings that you've described, did you ever hear presidents of the municipalities or representatives from municipalities express their concern with the presence of Serbian paramilitaries in their municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this subject was particularly prominent, although it was brought up at times. I don't remember any particularly heated debate on that. It was a matter for the municipalities to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember at any meeting you attended whether any representatives from Prijedor were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that meeting quite well, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You said you remember that meeting very well. Let's try to establish first of all when that meeting occurred. Do you remember, roughly speaking, when this was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact dates. This was a long time ago, and I didn't keep track of dates. But back then, there were problems with people arriving in the collection centres, in the surroundings of Prijedor, and several people were there who were from Prijedor, not just one person. That's why I remember the occasion well. There was a polemic during the debate with Mr. Radic about that, or rather how to resolve a number of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. What -- you've talked about collection centres in Prijedor. What came up at this meeting? What were you and anyone else present at the crisis staff informed of about these collection centres in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that there was a shortage of food, that they did not have sufficient accommodation or clothes to give those people; the usual problems that you encounter with collection centres, when you have a large number of people accumulated in one small area. That's what I found out about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What was your understanding -- according to the representatives from Prijedor, what was your understanding or -- let me back it up to make it clearer. What did the representatives from Prijedor tell you about these collection centres?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I remember this as a polemic, as a debate. I wasn't told anything personally. I wasn't personally addressed, but I do remember that there was a debate between someone - I can't quite remember who it was - but there were at least three persons from Prijedor taking part in this debate or clash. Given that they were not happy, or at least that was my understanding, with the way their requests had been met, and some were especially unhappy with the president of Banja Luka Municipality. I know that that's what the -- that was what the clash was about. But that's where it ended. It was only a verbal clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Did you become aware of Mr. Radic, the president of the Banja Luka Municipality, making a trip to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: This clash, this polemic, this debate that you have been talking about, did that occur before or after Mr. Radic's trip to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the meeting or the polemic - I may have used an inappropriate word, whatever - I believe that it happened before. But I'm not -- I'm no longer very clear about the dates. My assumption is that it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. During this debate, were you and other members of the crisis staff informed of the conditions in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was there any indication to you or any other member of the crisis staff about the maltreatment that was occurring in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When did you finally get a picture about what was actually happening in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I never went to any of the camps and collection centres, I got my impressions from the delegation who had been there and through my informal talk with Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Was Mr. Radic the first person to describe to you -- who was the first person to describe to you the actual conditions at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was his reaction? When you saw him, how was he reacting to the conditions and of what he saw out there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I describe his reaction? It was a negative reaction. He expressed regret for having gone there. He expressed regret for having gone there and seeing what he had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me go ahead. I'm going to talk to you about some of the conclusions now of the ARK Crisis Staff. Those documents are before you. The first document I'm going to talk to you about is P192. This is the decision -- excuse me, the conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff, 13 May 1992. It's in -- page 17 of the English version --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If we look at conclusion number 3, and it reads as follows: "On Saturday, 16 May 1992, a delegation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina consisting of Kupresanin, Erceg, Brdjanin, Radic, Sajic, Zupljanin, Kondic, Koruga, Sukalo is to told talks in Knin with representatives of the Serbian Republic of Krajina on establishing links and information and the economy." First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I'm not quite sure that the witness...

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: He has got 192 tabbed in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see the usher is -- have you found the excerpt? Usher, has he found it, or not yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Sorry to interrupt you, but I thought it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely no problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, please read that to yourself. I want to make sure you've had enough time to look at that. Once you're done reading it, please let me know because I want to ask you a question. I'm just talking about number 3 which talks about a trip to Knin with other members.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you go on this trip as part of a delegation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Tell us about that. Did you attend any meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'm not sure that all these people went. I'm not sure. Secondly, we flew by helicopter. We landed at Srnetica, a small abandoned place. It was abandoned during the previous state, previously, for previous economic reasons. There were buildings there that were in a state of delapidation. There was a railway there, a local railway -- actually, a local train called Ciro, and we spent some time there. I think it was a nice day. And we indulged in recreative activities, and then we went to Knin. I think we went to a sports ground, and then a part of the delegation had talks. They were presided over by Mr. Brdjanin. And during that time, I had a walk in Knin. I looked at windows, and at a given agreed time we returned. I spent some time in that room, but sincerely speaking, I didn't take part in the meeting, and I wouldn't remember what the topic of discussion had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So just to clear this up, when you say "I spent some time in that room," you're talking about the actual meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking of a room where we were to get together to return, and not where actually a meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you remember on either the trip up or the trip back any discussions about why this meeting was being held?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the aim of the meeting was to establish links between the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. representatives of the Serbian Republic of Krajina and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I can't be sure, but I had the feeling that the leadership from Pale condemned the meeting and, in fact, didn't pay much attention to the substance of the meeting. I think those were the comments following the meeting. As far as I was concerned, it was merely a trip to go there and come back and to have a nice time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You bring up the point that the leadership from Pale condemned the meeting. Generally speaking, if you know, what was Pale's attitude towards the ARK or the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't take part in any of the talks, but I had a feeling that they didn't wish any strong links between the two Krajina given the time frame. That was my personal feeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. What was -- the leadership in Pale, what was their attitude towards the ARK Crisis Staff? Did you ever see anyone from Pale attend a meeting of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see anyone attending the meeting, at least the ones I personally attended. The Minister of Defence would come to Banja Luka, and there were to have been talks and I was to be present, given my function as secretary of defence. I think that Mr. Brdjanin was present also, perhaps Nikola Erceg and someone else. But the talks weren't held on that particular day. I think the Minister of Defence spoke with the President of the Assembly of Banja Luka. But my feeling was that it didn't have a very positive view of the crisis staff. And the reorganisation of the Secretariat for Defence ensued. The Minister of Defence ordered that we restructure the Secretariat of Defence into departments, Drvar, Banja Luka, Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, I got you off track a little bit. Let's go back to the conclusions of 13 May 1992, which are contained in Prosecutor's Exhibit 192. If you go down to conclusion number 7, that conclusion reads as follows, 7: "The persons authorised to resolve all military and political issues in the Autonomous Region of Krajina are Vojo Kupresanin and Predrag Radic." Do you remember how it is that this conclusion came to be adopted?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember how it was adopted. I don't question that it was not or was adopted, that it had some sense or that one could expect something as a result. The political problems, well, Vojo Kupresanin was there, and the president of the Assembly of Banja Luka. That conclusion, in my view, and even now when I read it, is unrealistic and it's not really feasible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, do you have any sense, any idea, why Kupresanin and Radic were chosen to be the individuals resolving the military and political issues within the Krajina? Why them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Kupresanin, well, I could understand because president of the Assembly of Krajina. But as regards Radic, I'm not quite clear about that. He may have had some authority, or perhaps Radic's authority in view of the command of the corps. It could have been that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the conclusion number 9 in that same document, having to do with the transit of military convoys through the ARK, and it requires that transit of military convoys be reported to you and that, and I'm quoting now, "no military convoys coming from Banija are allowed through, and those coming from Bihac can be allowed through with Lieutenant Colonel Sajic." What was the impact if any of conclusion number 9 dealing with military convoys and giving you what appears to be certain responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that conclusion is not realistic at all. The convoys are controlled by the military, nothing to do with the secretary of defence, someone who works in the administration, who has no relation with that. I think that this was quite normal. Can I read --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Just read it to yourself so the interpreters -- if you're going to read something, just read it to yourself so the interpreters don't have to try to keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. My comment: The presidents of the National Defence Councils were usually presidents of the municipalities. They could not control the military convoys. They couldn't do that. They had no obligations to inform me. I had no competence in that respect. This was not our obligation, and my job has nothing to do with convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I've heard what you said, but even in spite of that, do you recall ever getting phone calls or having to arrange for convoys and approve convoys as reflected in this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If we go down to the very next conclusion, conclusion number 10 also discusses you, and it reads as follows: "Lieutenant Colonel Sajic is to produce an analysis of the situation at the Kosmos air force complex." First of all, what's the Kosmos air force complex? What is that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosmos air force complex is an institution which carried out repairs of aircraft, and it was under the competence of the military industry and the headquarters of the JNA. It is a company, a military enterprise in which active-duty officers were employed, and civilians, too, engineers, craftsmen, technicians, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Where is it located?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is located -- well, above the street where I live from Banja Luka in the direction of Jajce, on the way out of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What does it mean when it says that you are produce an analysis of the situation at the complex?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Brdjanin has information to the effect the state of affairs was not good there in the sense of different complaints by workers, in respect of the director who was a colonel or some other military person. And since it was a military company, I didn't refuse to carry out that task because I felt that I should speak with people in a normal fashion, and I did conduct such a talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when you went out there, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked with the director, and other people were also invited. And he told me that many people were complaining about different problems, their salaries. There was discontent among the workers. But that was the situation because Kosmos usually paid out high salaries, had good technology, but then it ceased to work because it no longer had to make repairs for different countries outside of Yugoslavia. And the -- this was the consequence of such a situation, and I drew the conclusion that actually no problems existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, were you ordered to go out there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How would you describe -- you said you were tasked to go out there. Why is it that you went out there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was said at that meeting that the situation there was not good. Then we decided who should go. It was proposed, whether it was the president of the crisis staff or someone else, that Sajic should go, because he was secretary of defence because he was familiar with questions of the army and defence. And I accepted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like for you to now turn to Exhibit P227. And I'm going to direct you -- it's on the English page -- in the English version it's on page 21. I'm talking about the conclusions of 18 May 1992. Exhibit 227 is the very thick one in your notebook in front of you. And I'm sorry, but I don't have the B/C/S page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's number 12, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't know if ... I can read the relevant portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: ERN P0049909 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me just read it and I'll have him comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, at the meeting of 18 May 1992 a conclusion was reached. I'm going to read it to you very carefully, very slowly, so please listen. Conclusion number 1 reads as follows: "A delegation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina consisting of Kupresanin, Erceg, Sajic, and Zupljanin is to go to Pale and hold talks on defining the territory towards Semberija." Do you remember that conclusion, first of all, being entered?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ever make the trip to Pale and hold these talks as reflected in this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you know if anyone ever went to Pale to hold these talks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know why this conclusion was entered?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understood it to be a delegation to discuss about what should be done next because there were hardly any links with Pale. They practically did not exist at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Links between who? Links between the ARK and Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how I understood that. I don't know to what extent they maintained links. I had no connection with Pale, and I went to Pale for the very first time when the war ended. My impression was that the links were very bad because links went through the centre -- actually, orders went through the centre. I was not in that delegation and I'm not able to comment what was said there because I simply was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question about your interview that you had with the Prosecutors in Banja Luka. Do you remember being asked whether the ARK Crisis Staff was the highest authority in the Krajina? Do you remember that question being put to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I'll put the very same question to you. Was the ARK Crisis Staff the highest authority in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two reasons, I believe: First, because I was convinced that the Pale leadership had some reservations, vis-a-vis Krajina, about the Assembly and all other bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Before you give us the second one, what caused you to come to the conclusion that the leadership in Pale had reservations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, their presence in that period was practically nonexistent, nonexistent. And secondly, I mentioned an event which -- I would speak with the leadership of Krajina, and the very feeling -- it still prevails today, that Pale is not very interested in Banja Luka. I think that they do not think this very important, that the leadership was up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I cut you off. You were saying -- you were giving two reasons why the ARK Crisis Staff was not the highest authority. The first one was that the leadership in Pale had reservations about the Krajina. What was the second basis for your conclusion that the ARK Crisis Staff was not the highest authority?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second reason, some municipalities did not accept any of the decisions and did not abide by the conclusions adopted there, first at the assembly and then subsequently the conclusions from the crisis staff. And the executive council, perhaps. I'm actually speaking about the municipality of Banja Luka, that they ignored them, and that the conclusions simply were not binding. It was something that I witnessed there. Whether some municipalities did accept those conclusions, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What was the most populous municipality in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What was Predrag Radic's attitude towards the crisis staff, the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't find it very important. He didn't -- he didn't really abide by those decisions very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I have just a minute, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. May I just inquire because I'm just feeling a little bit confused now. At the beginning of this sitting, we were each handed this pile of documents starting from DB319.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Those documents have absolutely nothing to do with this witness. Those are down the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: As Mr. Ackerman would say: "Don't worry about it now."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Nicholls, you could either start now with your cross, or we could have the break now, whichever you prefer. We are 17 and a half minutes away from the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can just start, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, today you've - and yesterday - you've spoken the truth to the best of your ability. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You told the truth, I suppose, when you spoke to the Defence team earlier and were interviewed by them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you remember, I think - it wasn't me - but speaking to members of the OTP in July 2001, and you spoke the truth all throughout that interview as well, didn't you, just as you have here today and yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think I read in your statement to the Defence that you had reviewed a portion of the transcript in your language from your interview with the OTP, and you confirmed that your words had been faithfully recorded; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But maybe there were some mistranslations. On the whole, though, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, well, from what you read, you said that everything had been faithfully recorded; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you arrived here in The Hague to testify, you were given a transcript in your language of the entire interview with the OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were allowed to review that in your hotel room?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Mr. Cunningham or somebody on the Defence team would have asked you if there were any major problems with that or any errors you saw; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just a little bit of your background; this will be very quick. You're now currently a professor; is that right? You're still teaching courses on defence and protection?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought you were. Are you now teaching courses on defence as well as being manager of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I no longer teach. I'm just the manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. When did you stop teaching?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never taught to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were in the TO or the VRS from 1968 through 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1969, following the completion of my military service, through 1992, June 1992. And after that, with the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And then with the VRS until 1996; is that about right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So really, much of your adult life you have been a professional, in the VRS, professional officer, and you were a professional in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you were a professional. You took your duties seriously. You were in there for about 30 years, and you did things as professionally as possible; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And part of that you learned, probably right in your basic service and all the way up until you retired from the VRS, the importance of clear, precise written orders in the military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And also, the importance of reporting up and down the chain to tell when orders had been received and whether they had been carried out, because the command needs to know that its orders have been acted upon; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think you'd agree with me that throughout your military career, either with the TO or with the VRS, you followed the rules - you were, as you said a professional - you were never involved in any kind of paramilitaries or commanding rogue units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the situation is similar, isn't it, with the police in the sense that with the CSB, there need to be clear orders that are precise; correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you'd agree -- well, Stojan Zupljanin, I've read many of his orders. You'd agree that he writes the type of precise, clear orders which are necessary.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read all of his orders, but that's how I imagine it to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, before we move on, you attended the 16th assembly session on the 12th of May, didn't you? That's the one where the VRS was formed.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think actually we have a videotape of that event, and you were sitting, were you not, next to General Talic in the front row who was sitting next to General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And basically, the entire RS leadership was present for that meeting, including Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am not sure whether the entire leadership, but on the whole, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, actually, Your Honour, maybe if I break now, I can get my documents straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we can break now. Usher, please could you escort the witness. We'll reconvene in 25 minutes' time. Thank you. Yes, there are these two motions that you referred to earlier on today. Have you had an occasion --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we didn't know anything about it either. We haven't got them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you try and get hold of them. I can give you mine, actually. And if there is no objection on your part, then we will decide them orally as soon as we reconvene.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, until we see them, we can't possibly say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Chuqing, you can hand these to... It's easier this way. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, let me -- this is not particularly important, but I just want to clear it up. Yesterday, you were asked, page 31, "do you have a university diploma, a university degree"? And the transcript says your answer was: "Yes, I have a BA in economy, and my other occupation is a teacher of national defence." Now, is that correct or not, that your other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I checked that myself earlier on, Mr. Nicholls. If you continue reading, I think you more or less have an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would suggest you skip that and you -- feel free to put the question. I'm not stopping you, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It was a degree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was on the same wavelength, and I checked it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I gave you a binder a moment ago and you've had about 5 minutes to look through it. That is a copy of the interview which you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in July 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In your language.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you now some questions which you've already -- about a topic you have been talking about, which are the ARK Crisis Staff meetings and the ARK Crisis Staff in general. Could you please go to page -- to tab 10; it's marked for you. It's page 55 of the English. We don't need to necessarily read through what all the questions and answers were, but your truthful statement in this interview was that Brdjanin presided over all meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the leading question .

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise .

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We might have called him, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. You gave me a fright, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You actually stated in that interview that the meetings couldn't even start unless Mr. Brdjanin was present; correct? Let me re-ask that question. I'll withdraw that. What you stated is: "What I wanted to confirm that he was in charge" -- he meaning Brdjanin -- "of all meetings. There was no one else, neither Nikola Erceg or anyone else." Correct? That's a truthful answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One of the other topics you talked about, and it wasn't entirely lear, I don't think, so we can talk about it a bit more, is bout how other -- people other than the named members of the crisis staff, ARK Crisis Staff, which you discussed at length with Mr. Cunningham, attended these meetings. If you go to tab 11 in your binder, you'll get to the section we're talking about. You don't need to refer to it unless you want to. But you were at several meetings, were you not, where in addition to the core to the ARK Crisis Staff membership, municipal presidents attended meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Could I get an English page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's page 59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm talking now about the corrected transcript. We had one come back late. We had somebody listen to it again to make sure. Did you understand my question, sir? Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So the answer is yes, you remember these people from ther municipalities attending; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in these meetings you stated in your opinion these meetings were more individually directed by Mr. Brdjo. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You remember Nedeljko Rasula attending these meetings, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, yes. One meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was his position during 1992? During the time that he was attending ARK Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the president of the Sanski Most Municipality Assembly, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he was president of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff, wasn't he? Municipal crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that he was the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Did you also know that he was president of the crisis staff during the time that the crisis staff or war staff of Sanski Most Municipality was in existence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have crisis staff on the one hand and war staff on the other. This is from my area of expertise, and these two are different. But very often these two are confused in documents. As a rule, according to the regulations then in force, it should have been the president of the executive council. But it's quite possible that it was the president of the assembly. I assume that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked about the representatives from Prijedor who you saw at these meetings. You weren't asked the names. Looking at your statement, does it refresh your memory? You remember now, who was there now, don't you? Dr. Milomir Stakic was present, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stated then and I confirm now that it is my belief that there were three persons from Prijedor whom I had not known before then, and I think that those were the people. In my statement to you, I think what I said was correct: Stakic, Kuruzovic, Drljaca. I think those were the three persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you know that -- you remember that Drljaca was the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time, but yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You also, and it's a little further on in the interview, you remember a Mr. Vasic from Prnjavor attending the meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Vasic. I don't know whether he attended that meeting. I don't think I said that. But if indeed I said that, then probably I remembered. He was, however, the president of Prnjavor Municipality at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And again, there were others whose names you don't remember who were present. This isn't an exhaustive list that we've just gone through. You need to answer verbally. I saw you nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you go to page -- tab 19, page 70 of the English. You talked about this on direct. There were quite a number of meetings that you know of of the ARK Crisis Staff, and the way these meetings were scheduled, you stated, is as follows: "It was up to Radoslav Brdjanin when he felt the need to organise or summon people to attend a meeting"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And these meetings, you would find out about the meeting via a telephone call.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said in your interview - it's at tab 20 if you want to look at it - and that's on the next page, for counsel, that these were often phone calls on short notice to attend a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go back to tab 16, please. This is on page 65 of the English. Now, very briefly, after these meetings had been held and people had spoken, Brdjanin formulated the conclusion or decision in relation to what had been discussed; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you look at tab 17 - it should be very nearby - I want to talk a little bit just briefly about what was discussed at these meetings. One of the first meetings or the first meeting you went to was on the 5th of May 1992. Right? About a day after you signed that order that we were talking about the other day.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One of the topics that was discussed extensively at that first meeting was the mobilisation process, the mobilisation which had just been ordered. That's the order you had passed down from the ministry at the republic level.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order on mobilisation was issued the day before. I still believe that we did not discuss mobilisation very much at this meeting, but we did probably discuss the disarmament of paramilitary units. However, I believe that the order on mobilisation was not on the agenda. As a rule, an order is not discussed once it has been issued and handed out. It is simply carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And you jumped ahead, but that's fine. Disarmament was something which was, as you stated in the interview, "surely discussed" at that first meeting. Right? That's what you were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in fact, the disarmament issue was one that was discussed frequently at ARK Crisis Staff meetings all through May, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the disarmament process went on all through May and into June; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Even now, they're not enforcing or talking about anything to do with your May 4th order, are they? Are they still running around looking for paramilitaries based on your order?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He said even now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't want to go through them all, but -- well, we can go through them quickly. On the 8th of May, there was -- let me give you P227. All right. Now, what you should have in front of you is the Official Gazette of the ARK from 5th of June 1992. Is that what you have?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the first item on the cover page is the 4th of May order with your signature on it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you go to conclusion number 4 - I'm sorry I can't give you the page - that's the 8th of May conclusions. Item 3 is about the disarmament of paramilitaries and states that "the strictest of sanctions will be imposed on those who refuse to return weapons."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll just ask you quickly; it's okay if you do or do not. Do you remember being present at the meeting where this conclusion was passed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me show you P182. Keep that binder with you. This is an ARK Crisis Staff conclusion -- decision, sorry, from the 9th of May, the one which states: "All the decisions and conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina are binding for all municipalities." Now, this decision makes all the other decisions - it's clear, it's very simply written - binding, doesn't it? That's what it states.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you look at the 9th of May ARK decision, which is in your book. It's number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you know which page of the English translation it's on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, because I'm using a different ERN copy. It's number 6, 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is, again, a conclusion about the disarmament process, and the deadline is again stated. "The weapons should be turned over to the nearest public security station by 1500 hours on 11 May at the latest. Firm action shall be taken against those who refuse to return weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's page 13 of the English, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So again, another discussion and conclusion drawn about the disarmament process; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you go to number 7, which is the 11th of May. This is on page 14 of the English -- 15 of the English. This conclusion is little more elaborate. "The deadline for the surrender of illegally acquired weapons has been extended to 14 May 1992 at 2400 hours." The next paragraph, I won't read it all because the Chamber has seen this many times before. But it has been extended on the basis of negotiations of citizens of all nationalities. And then, "After the deadline expires, weapons will be confiscated by employees of the Security Services Centre of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and severe sanctions will be imposed on those who ignore the call of the crisis staff." Do you remember the discussions about extending the deadline from the 11th of May to the 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. We're almost done. If you look at the 13th of May, that's conclusion 9, page 17 of the English. Number 4: "The Security Services Centre of Banja Luka is to fully implement the decisions of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on the disarming of illegal paramilitary units and individuals who are in possession of weapons and ammunition." This order talks about disarming paramilitaries and units and individuals; correct? It's a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we just saw this. This is the same conclusion that Mr. Cunningham asked you about and your visit to the Kosmos air force complex. Could you go to the 14th of May. That's decision number 10. Take a second and read that. Again: "Security Services Centre of the ARK is to fully implement the decision of the Crisis Staff of the ARK on disarming paramilitary units or individuals in unlawful possession of weapons and ammunition. Weapons are to be surrendered to police stations. Presidents of parties and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. community leaders should use their authority to influence citizens to return weapons." So again, another discussion and conclusion to implement the ARK decision to disarm; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Last one for now: Number 12 of the 18th of May, conclusions 3, 4, and 5. Number 3: "Illegal attained weapons will be taken away by members of the military and civilian police." Now, I think that's something you talked about yesterday, that that is, in fact, entirely correct in your view, that it would be the military and civilian police who would conduct this disarming exercise; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Number 4: "All formations that are not in the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Banja Luka Security Services Centre and are in the Autonomous Region of Krajina are considered paramilitary formations and must be disarmed." That's sort of in the negative way of defining all the people who are going to be disarmed, isn't it? If you're not in the army or the police, you're a paramilitary; you're going to be disarmed; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm object to the form of the question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: -- because that's not what's stated there. It talks about formations, not individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it's a fair question, and he has answered it. He read the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's read the next part. "All those who are not part of the armed force of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or its police must return their weapons." That's what it says there, sir, doesn't it? That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to your interview for a minute. Tab 18, sir, page 66 of the English. During your interview with us, you talked honestly about who was disarmed. You were asked, talking about the order on mobilisation and disarmament: "But the effect was this, wasn't it? That it was only the Muslims and Croats who were having their weapons removed from them." Your answer: "Mainly. You cannot say that it was a hundred per cent like that, but this statement can stand." And you were telling the truth, weren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were then asked about whether even those who had legal permits for hunting rifles and pistols had those weapons removed, and you told a story -- not a story, but you told as an example about a man you knew, a Muslim, who was disarmed by the police. He asked but it in advance "What do I do if the police come?". You said: "Things happen. As they happened, he referred to me. He mentioned my name. It didn't help. They removed his weapon." Right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were asked: "This gentleman was a Muslim." And you said: "Yes. Yes, a good Muslim."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was that in Banja Luka, this friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you go to tab 21 of your interview, sir. Now, here's where you talk about how camps were discussed at the ARK Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Can I get an English page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Page 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, here's the question you were asked: "There was never any time when meetings were held at 8.30 in the morning on a regular basis with a report being sent to Mr. Karadzic about what was discussed," talking about ARK Crisis Staff meetings. Your answer was: "I think that at one period, but I don't know which one, and the topic was predominantly camps, or centres, as they were called. Some people called them camps, some centres. Then I had the impression that such meetings of municipal presidents were supposed to be held, I think, at Mondays at 8.00." Do you remember giving that answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but -- but the answer was a longer one. We spoke about camps, economic problems, problems of supplies with fuels, and I said that today also.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I wasn't trying to imply that that was the only topic. I'm just reading you what your answer was, that you remembered camps being the topic --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- at one of these Monday morning meetings. And I think you're right about it being a Monday morning meeting because isn't it a fact that the presidents of the various municipalities of the autonomous region, either of the municipalities or of the crisis staffs in those municipalities, came to meetings in Banja Luka of the ARK Crisis Staff on Monday mornings so that on Tuesday mornings they could brief their municipalities on what was concluded or discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you stated later on, it's not particularly important, that you remembered that these Monday meetings were regular. Right? On page 72 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you talked about these camps -- when you talked about the meeting where camps were discussed, you said: "I was once present at the meeting when discussion was about prisoners." And then, as you said, there were other topics. Could you go to tab 23. That's on page 73, where I'm going. That's where you start talking about the visit to the collection centres, or camps. And you said: "Some of the members of the crisis staff visited those camps and collection centres." Plural. "This is primarily about the top few people." And then you go on to say who those top few people are. And state that you think it was Radic, Vukic, and Brdjanin who visited the camps; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said "camps" and "centres." Which other camps or centres besides Omarska did they visit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it here, but I was alluding to Omarska because I was only aware of that visit, and I only know the report about Omarska. Well, allow me to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take your time to read that, and while you're doing it, think about whether you ever heard or knew about - I'm not talking about you going there with them; I know you said I never visited any camps yourself - whether Mr. Brdjanin or Mr. Kupresanin visited Manteca, the 1KK prisoner camp --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me finish the question. Whether Mr. Brdjanin or Mr. Kupresanin visited the 1KK prisoner camp that was in Banja Luka? Do you know whether they visited there, whether together, separately, or in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you talked also about how Mr. Radic gave you his impression of his visit to Omarska. Who else was present during that -- during that meeting, or when he was talking to you about what he thought about Omarska, and saw there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was only me. I don't remember anyone else being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The -- you also talked about how when the people from Prijedor came and complained or argued with Mr. Radic, that was about the conditions in Omarska, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said something on direct about, well, you know, it was the usual problem of -- usual problems you get with collection centres. How do you know what the usual problems with collection centres are? You said that as though you knew a lot about running a collection centre and what the problems would be.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply believe the problems of the collection centres are identical in all centres, problem of food, accommodations, medical care. These are some fundamental problems that could exist there. It is not a conclusion based on my experience with those centres. The problems that occur when a larger number of people assemble at a certain point and in collection centres, the situation is even more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During that conversation with the Prijedor representatives, which turned into an argument, Radoslav Brdjanin was chairing that meeting as well, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go to tab 27, sir. It's page 82. I want to ask you a little bit about some of the things Mr. Brdjanin said when he was president of the ARK Crisis Staff, and perhaps just before he became president as well. One of the things you were asked about in this interview that you remembered was hearing from other Serbs that Mr. Brdjanin had said in the media -- doesn't say whether it's TV or radio -- that only a thousand Muslims will be allowed to stay in Banja Luka and that those thousand Muslims will be comprised of elderly people who will be put to cleaning the streets. Now, do you remember hearing about that from Serbs in Banja Luka, that they had heard Mr. Brdjanin say that in the media, as you state in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you remember, don't you -- you must remember from being in Banja Luka all of -- through April, May, June, July, and earlier, of 1992 -- that that wasn't an isolated comment. Mr. Brdjanin was famous, infamous, whatever, known, for making extremely nationalistic, disturbing comments along this nature, along the lines of this comment about Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You put too many adjectives together. I think you should reduce them a little bit or take them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just take you to your interview. That was a bad question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise. When you were asked -- this was at tab 28 for you, sir, page 83 -- about Vukic saying the same sorts of things as Brdjanin in the media, your response was: "Well, there was a group, the two of them, I don't know who else. They wanted to show themselves, expose themselves on television and radio." And then you say how these words weren't really thought through; right? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
